page.title: Building a load balancer
page.kicker: Lecture 05 · week 3, day 1 · running case: a load balancer you build yourself
page.dek: How to approach any distributed system, shown by building the box everyone draws and nobody opens, and then by locking things across machines.
page.description: Lecture 05: approach distributed systems by building a load balancer from one TCP proxy to a full control plane, then lock across machines with Redis and Redlock.

chapters.title: How to approach distributed systems
chapters.summary: A definition that holds up, the assumption that keeps a design honest, and the day-zero loop every real system grows by.

chapters.title: Choosing a backend: load balancing algorithms
chapters.summary: Round robin, weighted round robin and least connections, each tied to a kind of infrastructure and a kind of load.

chapters.title: A load balancer on one laptop
chapters.summary: Accept a TCP connection, open another, copy bytes both ways: the ten lines that make a load balancer, and how to run it locally.

chapters.title: The control plane: keeping every LB server right
chapters.summary: Configuration, health checks, pushing changes instead of polling, and metrics in Prometheus so the LB fleet can scale itself.

chapters.title: One name, many LB servers
chapters.summary: DNS answers and never forwards, private CoreDNS, the finished design with its two paths, and who watches the watcher.

chapters.title: Remote locks
chapters.summary: Three consumers, one queue that protects nothing: a lock on the network, why it must expire, and how not to delete someone else's.

chapters.title: Distributed locks
chapters.summary: When the lock store dies: a majority of five independent Redis nodes, its edge case, and why distributing is not scaling.

chapters.title: What to keep
chapters.summary: The heuristics from both halves, every box and how it stops being a single point of failure, and what comes next.
